items.question: Why do you think making frontier AI training infrastructure available to everyone is worth pursuing?
items.object: Making frontier AI training infrastructure available to everyone
items.answer: There's a lot of reasons. I think one is, and something that we are very passionate about, open science as a way that humanity moves forward, where a lot of the big scientific discoveries historically have been things that we talk about and as a world can build on top of. More practically speaking, there's a lot of value in model customization. The winning applications are using AI for a specific thing, for some agent, for some workflow, where you also want to be able to deliver this at scale and with cost-effective performance. The way to optimize these systems end to end is to have access to the model weights directly, where you can craft the model to be the best model for your problem rather than some model off the shelf where the crafting happens just in a prompt. It's allowing a deeper layer of customization than what you can do at the prompt level.

It's allowing a deeper layer of customization than what you can do at the prompt level.

The response states that direct access to model weights enables deeper task-specific customization than prompting an off-the-shelf model.

items.question: How do you envision companies developing their own AI research capabilities?
items.object: The future of in-house AI research at companies
items.answer: We definitely think that every company will be an AI company, and we think most AI companies will want to have an AI research lab. Research can look like many different things. It can look like pre-training, especially if you're in a domain where you maybe don't just want text in, text out. If you want something more bespoke. In a lot of cases it will be post-training agentic or otherwise focused models for specific tasks and workflows. I think that's getting to the point where it's productionizable and cost-effective, where you can actually make this very practical for people to do at scale for the right shape of problems that people want to solve.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between environments for model evaluation and environments for reinforcement learning?
items.object: Environments as a shared framework for model evaluation and training
items.answer: A big focus of Lab is the notion of an environment. A lot of people have heard the term environment in the context of reinforcement learning, and that's a big focus of it for us. An RL environment is encapsulating the things you need to do reinforcement learning, where you can have a model improve via trial and error. But it's also more general beyond just reinforcement learning. If you haven't heard of an environment before, it's essentially the same thing as the evals that get reported when people talk about new model releases. SWE-bench and AMIE and Terminal Bench are all examples of environments where there's a data set of tasks, a harness for the model to be in, and something called a rubric or reward function, which is responsible for grading the quality of the outputs. The same thing you'd use as an eval offline as your test set, you can use in reinforcement learning as your training set. This is a way to improve model performance interactively. Our platform is enabling people to use environments in their workflows for post-training, evaluation, synthetic data, and reinforcement learning.

items.question: How do you think about when to build dedicated reinforcement learning environments versus making the agent application itself the environment?
items.object: Dedicated RL environments versus using an agent application as the environment
items.answer:
I think there's definitely reasons where you want both. Especially, let's say you're training a model to be a really good Rust coding model. Here you might want it to be good for lots of different applications where you'd have different environments focused on some domain task. Maybe you're a company that wants a model that's going to be really good at calling your tools or using your specific domain language that you can provide as a service to people who are building around that.

Then there's also ones where the product very much is a user interface for an end user, where the user's interacting with an agent, in which case it might make the most sense for the product to very directly become the environment. I think the companies who might want to be doing this are the same who care about whether they're using Claude or GPT-5 or Gemini, or the ability to choose models and have internal systems to evaluate whether a certain system prompt is good, whether changing out a model endpoint is good, or whether using the mini version of a model is a better cost-performance trade-off. The infrastructure to do that is what a lot of people have already been building at these advanced agent companies. It's the same infrastructure you use to do reinforcement learning.

I think that's a convenient world we ended up in, where the training paradigm that makes the most sense for improving model capabilities is the same sort of thing that a lot of people have been building up the muscle for, just without doing the training piece. That's where we see RL being a very useful tool for people to have as an option in their toolkit for system optimization.

items.question: How do you think about agent harnesses in relation to RL environments?
items.object: Agent harnesses and the environment abstraction in reinforcement learning
items.answer:
They definitely relate. I think of a harness as a piece of the environment. For any eval or environment task, there's some input, a bunch of stuff is going to happen, then there's some output state which is then going to be graded. This whole intermediate piece, whether it's interacting with some simulator, some other agent, or a physical world sim, is the environment, and the harness is very much a piece of that which couples how the model interacts with any other pieces of the system.

Depending on the application area, for coding agents we have a pretty clear definition: you could say the harness is the CLI coding agent and the terminal is the environment. But this isn't necessarily universal across all different types of agents. In some cases it's a system prompt and some tools; in some cases it's something that is going to be spawning sub-agents, and the sub-agents also have their own harnesses. There's a lot of complexity, but harnesses are going to keep evolving. There's going to be this Cambrian explosion of ways people want to use models, and we want to take a pretty general approach in defining what you could do with a harness. That's why we use the term environment as the abstraction: agent is too narrow, harness is kind of too narrow, and you can do all of these things within an environment. The environment as an abstraction on the whole allows any sort of system-model interaction to be in scope.

items.question: Why do you see environments as a useful abstraction beyond reinforcement learning?
items.object: Environments as an abstraction beyond reinforcement learning
items.answer: I think environments are tools you can use to do all of these things. When I talk about environments beyond RL, part of the reason it's a useful abstraction is because it doesn't tie you to RL. Let's say I want to have a small model and I want it to be distilled from a big model. You plug the big model into your environment and let it run a bunch of times. Now you have a lot of this data that comes from the same interaction protocol. You can use the same grader at the end to filter for the best examples and then do SFT fine-tuning on that. You could do prompt optimization with an environment. You could A/B test different models with an environment, as you would with an eval. The idea is that every AI company should be optimizing their AI systems.

items.question: How do you think about the distinction between an evaluation and an environment for improving an AI model?
items.object: The distinction between evaluations and environments for improving AI models
items.answer: I think it depends on what you want to call it. In traditional machine learning terms, you don't want to overfit to the test set. In some ways we kind of are already accepting that we're going to be using the test set or the eval to measure, to have that kind of filter back into the model. It's a little tricky to distinguish even what is the eval and what is the environment. We kind of think of them as one and the same. We use the environment term very generically, where an eval is a type of environment that's used for measuring performance but not training on. A lot of people, when they're doing evals, have some way of measuring current performance and they're iterating on it. In some ways RL is this iteration applied at scale, where you're automatizing the process of changing the model a little bit, changing the prompts a little bit, and having this be the way that you can hill-climb on some goal.

items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning’s role in the broader process of post-training a model for deployment?
items.object: Reinforcement learning’s role in post-training
items.answer: I think reinforcement learning is the big thing now. In many cases, practically speaking, if you're doing a large-scale model, RL will be where you spend most of your time, focus, and compute. But it's not the only thing you want to do. There's a lot involved in the whole process of going from some initial model to the system you want to deploy. This can be prompt tuning, SFT, online distillation. There are a number of algorithms that all kind of are under this umbrella, where RL is the big one in the middle, but there's a lot of stuff around it.

items.question: What do you see as the key value of Prime Intellect's platform for medical AI labs such as OpenMed?
items.object: Prime Intellect's platform for medical AI labs such as OpenMed
items.answer:
We work closely with a number of groups in the medical AI space where they want to create benchmarks to understand how good models are at medical capabilities, both in terms of diagnosis or patient interactions or question answering about medical literature, or agentic search over certain medical tasks.

So far, OpenMed is one that we work closely with. They really care about earning trust from medical professionals. They want to focus on the domain and not as much on the generic medical LM infrastructure that's a headache for a lot of people. For them, having this platform for creating evaluations, showing them off, using them to improve model capabilities that could then be deployed locally in a hospital or for some end user, is useful. The ability to have this customization and end-to-end trust and understanding of the data provenance for tasks at hand, or the ability to customize models very directly, is key.

items.question: Why do you find Wordle useful as a demonstration environment for reinforcement learning with language models?
items.object: Wordle as a demonstration environment for reinforcement learning with language models
items.answer: One fun one that I use as a demo a lot is Wordle from the New York Times. This ended up being a great hello-world environment because the infrastructure is really simple but expressive, where you can get a feel for it and get this aha moment of seeing a model learn to think about the game as you give it rewards for doing better. You can do it with a really tiny model too. It's in the sweet spot of difficulty where you can do these runs on a couple GPUs in an hour and see a model actually learn how to get better at the game.

items.answer: One fun one that I use as a demo a lot is Wordle from the New York Times. items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning helping to vet training environments before they reach a frontier model's training run?
items.object: Reinforcement learning as a way to evaluate data and training-environment quality
items.answer: We work with a lot of people in the data and environment space, where we found a lot of interest in using reinforcement learning as a way to evaluate data quality. The ability to measure what happens when you train a model on a set of tasks, rubrics, and environments allows you to understand bugs in the environments, because there are issues that come up in reinforcement learning where maybe if your environment has a backdoor, a model can exploit this and game the system. There's a lot of interest in people using RL in the pipeline from idea to an environment that ends up in some frontier lab's foundational training run for the next GPT or Claude model. There's a lot of vetting that goes into this. Doing these smaller or medium-scale runs in one environment allows you to poke and see where the problems might be.

items.question: How do you think about making simulated environments for AI agents realistic enough while keeping them efficient to run?
items.object: The complexity and cost of simulated environments for training AI agents
items.answer:
I would say there's less of a barrier in terms of the actual complexity. In principle these can be as complex as you want. It's anything that could be on a computer. Think of anything that's on a computer or a network of computers as potentially an environment. What really becomes the bottleneck in many ways is the cost of the simulator. I think there's a lot of focus on identifying clever ways to mock the right piece of the system.

Let's say you have an agent that you want to do a lot of web search. In some cases you actually want to do the real web search. In some cases you want to find ways where you can design tasks where you don't need the full thing. I think of the map games where there's this world you want to explore, where some of it's dark, but as you walk around the light shines and you now see this part of it. If you know which pieces of this map might actually be explored on a given task, this allows you to decide which pieces are important or not.

One example: there's a benchmark called Tattoo Bench that's very popular in the eval world, about customer service agents involving a database. In a real system you might need the full database, but if you know the agent is only going to ask certain types of questions for a task, you don't need a full database with millions or thousands or billions of records. You can have a mock database that's cheaper to run, maybe an in-memory piece of software, that only has the things expected by the agent or in the scope for a given task. Identifying the pieces of the system where the complexity is overkill is part of this task design process to enable efficiency.

items.question: How do you design your agent environment infrastructure to accommodate increasing complexity across different domains?
items.object: Designing infrastructure for increasingly complex agent environments
items.answer:
It's definitely a way that we think about the design of everything. We go down a lot of these different rabbit holes as we focus on different tasks from working with different people. Coding agents maybe are one example, where there's a lot of complexity that comes up when working with sandboxes and terminal states and ensuring that you have good snapshotting and protocols to interact with different agent harnesses. We've built a lot around that, but we know that the space of complexity is going to grow arbitrarily over time as people get deeper into these different domains.
We've tried to design everything in a way where we keep a lot of doors open, where we have room to build features. There are base layers of generic environments, then you can say, “I want a coding agent environment. I want a coding agent environment with a sandbox that's global across the run. I want one per rollout.” There are lots of different branches you can go down. We've anticipated there will be a lot of these branches. There are some we've built for, and some that I think we're ready to build for when we need to.

items.question: How do you think about creating a good developer experience for researchers using coding agents to build agent environments?

items.answer: We also think a lot about how to make a good developer experience. Think about documentation or skill files for agents. People are going to be using coding agents when they're building these. There's a lot of institutional knowledge that gets built up when you're doing this kind of research, both for a specific project or as a research team doing large-scale training runs. Being able to surface this information, some of it is directly in the product, some of it in the way we design the libraries, some in documentation or skill files that get shown to agents. items.question: Do you see constructing RL environments as the natural successor to the kind of human data labeling associated with Scale AI?
items.object: RL environment construction as a successor to human data labeling
items.answer:
It very much seems like it already is. A lot of the focus from the major labs has shifted. They're still using a lot of human data, and human data doesn't seem to be going away, because creating these environments is by definition for things that models aren't good enough at yet, which means the humans are better than the models in some capacity.
Identifying which pieces of information the human can most uniquely assist the model in improving its skill on, I think, is really the key to target: how do you create this information flow from the human who has the expert knowledge on how to do something, what a job well done looks like, and get it into the model? RL seems to be the most effective way to do this right now, where having tasks with prompts to grade with an LM judge, a rubric for what success looks like on a task, is the paradigm that's emerging for a lot of these cases. Sometimes it's through a reward model, but the most direct, visceral version is a set of yes/no questions: was this done in the LM's answer? That turns into the reward score. That requires a lot of human data.

items.question: What value do you see in an RL environment hub for people who keep their environments private?
items.object: The value of an RL environment hub for users with private environments
items.answer: There's definitely a lot of people we work with who want to keep their environments private, as you understand. But the value for them of it being a hub is that they can do ablations and compare their private one versus some public one that might be on a similar type of task. For evals, there's a lot of value in having uniform implementations of popular benchmarks so that if you're doing a training run, you can plug in some known eval to monitor the progress of your run. Maybe you're doing well on your environment; you can see whether your environment also generalizes to other tasks. Having all these other tasks available is a really helpful way for people to understand not just their own task, but other things they might want the model to be good at as well.

items.question: Where do you see the value in Wiki Search as a template for agentic search?
items.object: Wiki Search, an RL environment template for agentic search
items.answer: I think one where we've seen a lot of interest and the most branching and forking into different versions is one we call Wiki Search, which is doing search over Wikipedia pages but is designed as a template you could use for agentic search more broadly. There's a lot of applications where people want agents that know how to search over their internal documents or documents for a specific type of information. That's the sort of thing where we see a lot of value in people bringing other types of documents they'd want to do agentic search over.

items.question: How do you think about the value of reinforcement learning given how much compute it uses to obtain a small information signal?
items.object: Reinforcement learning's compute efficiency and value
items.answer:
I think it's definitely true that RL is using a lot of compute to get a pretty small signal in terms of pure information. But in some ways that's part of the value of it as well, and one of the reasons a lot of the labs have really focused on it is that one of the bottlenecks that's hard to scale is human data, especially high-quality human data. RL allows you to trade off compute for data, where you can get a lot of value out of a smaller amount of data by using more compute. The supervision coming from this data is small, but you can get a lot out of it, more so than via pre-training or supervised fine-tuning alone.
It's useful in cases where you don't necessarily have golden examples. If you have a bigger model to distill from, that's great. But if you're already at the biggest model size you have access to, then you need to go into untrodden territory, and exploration is really the heart of RL. How do you explore and try out different things? Maybe there are ways to do exploration that are more efficient than RL that people will discover, but this is currently the frontier of using compute to explore and improve capabilities. It's what we got for now.

items.question: How do you see Prime Intellect’s environment infrastructure being useful for research on closed-weight models?
items.object: Prime Intellect’s environment infrastructure for research on closed-weight models
items.answer: In many ways, the trainer itself is going to require having access to the weights, so if anyone who has closed-weight models wants to use it, we're happy to chat. There's a lot of research that can be done around closed models just by having a way to do this experimentation.

items.question: How do you think about choosing between a LoRA adapter and full fine-tuning for reinforcement learning?
items.object: LoRA and partial model customization for reinforcement learning
items.answer: I would consider LoRA still part of the fine-tuning process, and that's what we recommend a lot of people do for RL anyways. You don't need that necessarily with the full weights, but you can't upload your own LoRA for GPT-5. But I could bring an environment to the platform, potentially. I think there are a lot of different ways you can do partial customization, and I would imagine that in many cases whether you need a LoRA adapter or full fine-tuning is going to depend on the training recipe as well as the goal of your optimization.

items.question: What excites you about synthetic data research as a direction for continual learning?
items.object: Synthetic data research for continual and lifelong learning
items.answer: I'm really excited about synthetic data research. It feels like there's a lot of stuff that we should be able to do, but you haven't really seen it emerge in the open in terms of creative ways of doing self-reflection. People talk a lot about continual learning as this idea that we're going to have to get better at models learning things on their own. Using other tricks that we already know in conjunction in different ways—things like prompt optimization, distillation, in conjunction with synthetic data—feels like there's a lot of room for exploration around having models curate their own training data, maybe curate their own environments, and understanding which versions of this are most effective for lifelong learning.

items.question: How do you think about the value of enabling every company to do its own AI training?
items.object: Enabling companies to train AI and compound institutional knowledge
items.answer:
In some ways, if data is the bottleneck, if having the real expertise is the bottleneck, would you rather have the smartest person in history work at your company or someone who's been there for 30 years? Sometimes you really want the person who's been there for 30 years. There's a lot of expertise that comes from really understanding a problem deeply and interacting with it over a long time. This is really what happens in training that is almost impossible to replicate in a short prompt. You really want the ability for institutional knowledge to compound over time, for best practices to compound over time. This is how institutions and companies grow to be really powerful and successful: they stand on the shoulders of what they've done before rather than resetting every day.
We want to have this be accessible to any company that wants to do this. That's how we've thought about approaching it, especially as software becomes easier for people to manipulate, as the barrier to entry for coding becomes easier. We see the same happening for AI research.
